title: Learn Without a Manual
statement: A first-time player should be moving before reading anything.
summary: Designed the tower's screens so the controls are found by playing, then watched people play and fed every stuck point back into the design.

detail.problem: A large RPG (104 floors, over a thousand items) can bury a new player under rules and menus before the fun starts.
detail.designMove: Keep a single line of instruction on screen and let the map, items and characters teach the rest. Treat every place a tester stops as a design bug.
detail.outcome: In the first playtest, a family member learned the controls in about three minutes with no explanation and cleared a five-floor section.

media.alt: Tower floor with the billboard panel showing one line of controls.

title: Tools Before Content
statement: A world grows faster when the people filling it never touch code.
summary: Built in-house authoring desks (NPC sheet, scene, item, enemy and price tables, and NESI for dialogue and events) so the game is edited as data.

detail.problem: Content lived inside one 36,000-line game file. Each new character or item was slow to add, easy to break, and blocked several AI agents from working at the same time.
detail.designMove: Move content out of code into tables, each with its own editor showing the same IDs the game uses. Split the engine into 69 source files that are assembled back into one at build time.
detail.outcome: Characters went from 14 to 139 in one month, with three consistency passes. 41 tools now feed the game.

media.alt: NPC sheet editor: list of characters on the left, one character's settings on the right.

title: A Livehouse in the Tower
statement: The game and the music are one world, not two products.
summary: Designed an in-game livehouse where a band of characters plays songs from my own releases, with crowd cheers, an encore and stage lights.

detail.problem: The game had 34 tracks of background music made only for the game, separate from the songs released on the music site.
detail.designMove: Replace game-only music with released songs played through an in-game player, and turn listening into a place: a ticketed livehouse inside the tower.
detail.outcome: Game and music now share one catalog, and an in-game ticket ($1.99) connects playing the game to the band.

media.alt: The tower as it looks in the browser.

title: Buy Without an Account
statement: Buying a song should take one step, and losing it should not be possible.
summary: Designed a store where songs are bought without signing up, kept in the browser, and brought back by email.

detail.problem: Making an account is where most small music purchases are dropped. Without accounts, clearing the browser would mean losing what you bought.
detail.designMove: Keep ownership in the browser for instant access, and make email the way back: one address restores every purchase.
detail.outcome: Payment, storage, delivery and mail run through Stripe, R2, Upstash, Resend and Vercel. Purchase, download and email recovery pass end to end in test mode.

media.alt: Music site with the release grid on the left and the player on the right.

title: Owned Things Simply Appear
statement: What you bought shows up as an object, not a line in a list.
summary: Releases are shown as CDs and a record player. The listening room on the home page does not exist until you buy something: it is not greyed out, it is absent.

detail.problem: Digital purchases usually sit in a grey library list that feels like nothing was bought, and an empty listening-room button tells new visitors about a feature they can't use.
detail.designMove: Show owned releases as physical objects, and keep the listening room off the home page until there is something in it, instead of showing a disabled button.
detail.outcome: The home page stays clean for new visitors and gains a listening room, "everything you own, in one room", the moment a purchase happens.

media.alt: rec.ooo home before and after a purchase: the listening room icon appears.

title: A Dock That Never Says No
statement: When the dock is full, adding still works: the oldest icon leaves.
summary: Visitors build their own dock of up to 14 icons from the site's list.

detail.problem: An earlier version stopped drawing the add buttons when the dock was full. Every button in the list vanished at once, which looked like a bug and broke the first screen's promise that you can add freely.
detail.designMove: Never block. When the dock is full, push the oldest icon out (first in, first out).
detail.outcome: Adding always works, and the promise on the first screen stays true.

media.alt: rec.ooo home: grouped list on the left, intro panel and dock icons on the right.

title: Failure Without Words
statement: A wrong answer gets a symbol, not a sentence.
summary: Hidden entries open with a keyword. A failed attempt gets a half-second ❌ at the input, and no error message.

detail.problem: Error text like 'wrong password' explains the gate and turns a quiet hidden entry into a puzzle with instructions.
detail.designMove: Remove the warning layer. Flash ❌ once at the point of input; after that, nothing.
detail.outcome: Visitors know the attempt didn't pass, and hidden entries stay hidden.

media.alt: Locked career entry asks for an initial; a wrong answer returns without any message.

title: Copy for People Standing Up
statement: Phone users get their own words, not cut-off desktop sentences.
summary: Every entry has a second, very short text for mobile, written like a small child who only knows a few words.

detail.problem: The mobile screen is a small fixed square, and people scroll it standing up. The desktop sentences don't fit and aren't read.
detail.designMove: Write a separate short copy for every entry instead of truncating the long one. The two are edited independently.
detail.outcome: Every public entry has a mobile version, and desktop keeps its full sentences.

media.alt: rec.ooo on a phone: short greeting and a grid of icons.

title: Same Input, Same Result
statement: A formatting tool you can trust has to be boringly predictable.
summary: A text tool that formats by fixed rules, with no AI at run time.

detail.problem: AI rewriting gives a different result each time, so you can't review what changed or rely on it for the next document.
detail.designMove: Make every rule explicit and deterministic, and keep each change traceable to the rule that made it.
detail.outcome: The same input always gives the same result. The how-to post has been shared more than 50 times.

media.alt: kiln projector switching presets on the same input and back.

title: Design the File First
statement: Before drawing the tree, decide what a tree is.
summary: A tool that lays out ideas and documents as a tree. The .root file format (JSON schema ruvia-doc/0.1) was designed before the interface.

detail.problem: Thinking tools often lock content inside their own interface; anything written elsewhere, including by AI, has to be rebuilt by hand.
detail.designMove: Define the saved format first, so documents written by AI import as they are. Separate display names from internal IDs, so renaming never breaks links.
detail.outcome: Ideas move in and out as plain files; the tree view is one way to read them.

media.alt: New knots get an ID first (knot-a-d), then their content is written.

title: Session Stream
statement: AI work unfolds as a continuous workspace rather than a series of closed sessions.
summary: Designed a mobile-first navigation model in which documents, conversations, and active contexts are traversed through continuous vertical movement instead of repeated session switching.

detail.problem: Conventional AI interfaces split work into separate sessions, forcing users to repeatedly enter, exit, and reconstruct context across isolated views.
detail.designMove: Recast sessions as positions inside a single spatial stream, so movement across tasks happens through scrolling rather than through container changes.
detail.outcome: Shifts conversation from session management to spatial navigation, making context easier to retain, revisit, and work across.

media.alt: Mobile interface showing continuous scrolling between AI sessions and documents.

impact: Turns multi-session interaction into a spatial navigation model.

title: Meta Control
statement: System behavior is edited in context through language instead of hidden control panels.
summary: Designed an interaction layer where users can change document type, access state, and behavioral rules directly from within the workspace using natural language.

detail.problem: In most systems, configuration is pushed into secondary panels and technical metadata flows, separating operational control from the work itself.
detail.designMove: Placed behavioral control inside the primary interface by letting users issue structural changes in language, with explicit application states that keep the system legible.
detail.outcome: Turns configuration into a first-class interaction, allowing system behavior to be modified where the work is actually happening.

media.alt: User changing document type and metadata through natural language commands.

impact: Makes system-level behavior editable through interaction instead of hidden configuration.

title: Header System
statement: Documents operate as active system objects rather than passive files.
summary: Designed a document model where structured headers define execution logic, permissions, and system behavior, making control state readable and editable as part of the document itself.

detail.problem: Most software separates content from behavior, leaving users to navigate between the document they are working on and the hidden structures that determine how it behaves.
detail.designMove: Promoted the document header into an explicit control surface, so the governing logic of a document can be inspected, modified, and applied in place.
detail.outcome: Repositions documents as programmable interface units whose structure is directly usable rather than concealed in the system layer.

media.alt: Document header being modified and applied as a control layer.

impact: Turns documents into active components of system behavior.

title: Ghostwriting
statement: AI assistance appears inside the draft instead of in a separate conversational channel.
summary: Designed an in-place co-writing mode where generated output is inserted directly into the document, keeping composition and assistance inside the same working surface.

detail.problem: Typical AI writing tools split drafting and assistance across two interfaces, which breaks writing flow and turns revision into a context-switching task.
detail.designMove: Collapsed the editor and the assistant into one surface, so generation happens exactly where the text is being written and revised.
detail.outcome: Produces a co-writing model in which AI behaves as part of the drafting environment rather than as an external sidecar.

media.alt: AI writing directly inside a text document alongside user input.

impact: Integrates AI into the writing surface instead of separating it.
